text: Every IT department plans and delivers work using one of two basic shapes, or some blend of both — and before you can understand a Jira ticket, a sprint, or a change-control form, you need to know which shape the team around you is using.

Waterfall plans an entire project up front, then moves through fixed phases once, in order — requirements, design, build, test, release — each phase finishing before the next starts. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating cycles, typically one to two weeks, where the team plans, builds, reviews, and adapts every single cycle.

The five-phase Waterfall diagram is the simplified shape — a sixth phase, Maintenance, almost always follows Release in practice. It's easy to forget when a plan is first pitched, but maintenance is usually the longest phase of a system's entire life, which is why asking who maintains this after launch is worth asking before a project ever starts.

Agile's cycle doesn't run once — it chains forward, sprint after sprint, each one picking up where the last sprint's retrospective left off. The system never finishes a single design phase the way Waterfall does; design keeps happening a little at a time, every cycle.

Few companies are purely one or the other. A common hybrid keeps Waterfall's up-front charter and final sign-off for budgeting and executive buy-in, while running the actual build in Agile sprints in between — which is exactly why you'll hear both vocabularies at the same company.
Next lesson: Scrum, the specific named framework most teams mean when they say they're Agile — the roles, the meetings, and the vocabulary you'll actually hear in a standup.
